issues.legal_issue: A writ of quo warranto cannot be issued on suspicion of ineligibility while the certificate supporting the holder’s eligibility remains valid and the disputed eligibility facts await determination by the competent authority.
material_facts: The elected office was a public office, and the officeholder relied on an income and caste certificate issued by the competent authority to contest the reserved position.
The certificate had not been cancelled or invalidated, and its validity was pending before the caste verification committee.
The challenge relied on discrepancies alleged between affidavits and on circumstances surrounding the certificate’s issuance; the courts below did not find the certificate void.
The Supreme Court found no indisputable facts establishing that the officeholder was ineligible or disqualified.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not issue quo warranto while the certificate remained valid and the alleged ineligibility remained unresolved. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court decisions and directed the competent committee to expedite its inquiry and decide the certificate’s validity independently and in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Quo warranto is a limited and discretionary remedy to determine whether a person holds a public office without legal authority. It ordinarily requires indisputable facts establishing statutory ineligibility or disqualification; suspicion, inference, or disputed facts are insufficient. A certificate remains operative until invalidated by the competent authority under the applicable statutory scheme. The Court relied on Article 226 of the Constitution; the certificate’s statutory presumption of validity under Rule 3-C of the 1992 Rules; University of Mysore v. C.D. Govinda Rao; Nawabkhan Abbaskhan v. State of Gujarat; K. Venkatachalam v. A. Swamickan; Kurapati Maria Das v. Ambedkar Seva Samajan; Arun Singh v. State of Bihar; B.R. Kapur v. State of Tamil Nadu; High Court of Gujarat v. Gujarat Kishan Mazdoor Panchayat; Mor Modern Coop. Transport Society Ltd. v. Financial Commissioner; and the related quo warranto authorities discussed in the judgment.

rule.if: quo_warranto_challenge and certificate_valid_and_uncancelled and (eligibility_facts_disputed or disqualification_not_indisputable)

predicates.quo_warranto_challenge: A proceeding seeks removal of a person from a public office by questioning that person’s authority to hold it.
predicates.certificate_valid_and_uncancelled: The officeholder relies on an officially issued eligibility certificate that has not been cancelled or invalidated by the competent authority.
predicates.eligibility_facts_disputed: The asserted ineligibility depends on contested facts that remain for determination by the competent authority.
predicates.disqualification_not_indisputable: The established facts do not conclusively show that the officeholder was ineligible or disqualified.

issues.definition: When a quo warranto challenge depends on disputed eligibility facts and the supporting certificate remains operative without an indisputable disqualification, the holder cannot be ousted by that writ.

issues.legal_issue: The short time taken to issue an eligibility certificate does not, by itself, establish that the required procedure was not followed or justify invalidating the certificate.
material_facts: The application was processed over several days rather than issued on the application date.
The official file showed that a notice was issued, a report and mahazar were prepared, a statement was recorded, and supporting documents were collected.
The certificate was issued on the day the affidavit was notarized, and the lower courts relied on the speed of the process and other circumstances to doubt its genuineness.
issues.conclusion: The five-day processing period, even though short, was not by itself a sufficient basis to infer that the required procedure had not been followed or to invalidate the certificate; the competent committee had to examine the procedure and eligibility in its inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: The validity of the certificate and compliance with the prescribed procedure are matters for the competent verification authority to determine on the evidence. A short processing period alone does not establish procedural failure. The Court applied the statutory verification framework under the 1990 Act and the Rules framed under it, including the principle that the certificate remains valid until cancelled by the competent authority.

predicates.certificate_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges whether an officially issued eligibility certificate is valid.
predicates.certificate_processed_within_short_perio: The competent authority issued the certificate a relatively short time after receiving the application.
predicates.required_processing_steps_documented: The official record shows that procedural steps and supporting inquiries occurred before the certificate was issued.

issues.definition: In a challenge to a certificate, a short processing period accompanied by documented procedural steps does not, without more, establish procedural failure.

issues.legal_issue: A tax-based exclusion from reserved-category eligibility depends on whether the specified person is an assessee for the relevant period, and the spouse’s income alone does not satisfy that condition.
material_facts: The applicable reservation note excluded a person if that person or either parent or guardian was an income-tax or wealth-tax assessee.
The challenge relied on an earlier affidavit stating that the officeholder was an income-tax assessee and on reported rental and family income.

The officeholder maintained that the affidavits concerned different financial periods, and the Court found no material showing that the officeholder or the relevant parents or guardians had paid, or were liable to pay, tax for the relevant period.
The Court stated that the spouse’s income was not a relevant fact under the wording of the exclusion and left the factual eligibility determination to the verification committee.
issues.conclusion: The verification committee had to determine whether the officeholder or a parent or guardian was an assessee on the relevant date, applying the relevant tax-law meaning of assessee; past tax status or the spouse’s income alone did not establish ineligibility.
issues.legal_principle: The exclusion in Clause (ii) of the note to the reservation notification must be strictly construed. Its present-tense wording concerns whether the specified person is an assessee for the relevant period, meaning a person who pays or is liable to pay tax or another sum under the relevant tax law; it does not make the spouse’s income independently relevant. The Court considered the applicable notification and the principles in K. Krishna Murthy (Dr.) v. Union of India and Indra Sawhney v. Union of India, while leaving the ultimate factual determination to the caste verification committee.

predicates.reserved_category_eligibility_review: A competent body is reviewing a person’s eligibility for a reserved public position under a tax-based exclusion.
predicates.relevant_period_tax_status_unproven: There is no established evidence that the person or a specified parent or guardian paid or was liable to pay tax for the relevant period.
predicates.spouse_income_is_the_only_tax_related_ba: The asserted tax-related ground for exclusion is the spouse’s income rather than the tax status of a person specified by the eligibility condition.

issues.definition: In a reserved-category eligibility review, unproven relevant-period tax status and reliance only on the spouse’s income do not establish tax-based ineligibility.
